subject: geography
book: Fundamentals of Physical Geography; India: Physical Environment (NCERT, rationalised) [practical: Practical Work in Geography Part I]

sections.name: 1.1 Introduction: geography and the earth's surface

concepts.text: Earth as home of humans: varied physical features and cultural features across space
Meaning of geography: description of the earth; term coined by Eratosthenes (geo = earth, graphos = description)
Geography as the study of the earth as the home of humankind
Geography studies areal differentiation: how places differ and resemble each other
Physical environment and cultural environment; humans interact with and modify nature over time

sections.name: 1.2 Geography as a discipline: the What, Where and Why questions

concepts.text: Geography concerned with spatial attributes and the spatial perspective
Three core questions: what (patterns of features), where (distribution/location) and why (causal explanation)
Geography as the study of interrelationships and associations between phenomena in space
Dynamic relationship between nature and humans: technology loosening the shackles of nature
Environmental determinism (naturalisation of humans) vs humanisation of nature; level of technology as an index of culture
Possibilism and changing human perception of the environment
Geography as a discipline of synthesis rather than a study of isolated facts
Geography as a discipline of spatial synthesis; history as a discipline of temporal synthesis
Link with natural sciences: geomorphology-geology, climatology-meteorology, biogeography-botany/zoology, soil geography-pedology, oceanography
Link with social sciences: economics, political science, sociology, history, demography, anthropology
Maps as the main tool of geographers; cartography, quantitative methods, remote sensing and GIS as techniques
Diagram idea: geography's links with other disciplines (Figure: geography and its relation with other subjects)
Physical and human phenomena described with metaphors from each other (e.g. 'face of the earth', 'eye of the storm', 'mouth of a river')
Two approaches: systematic approach (Humboldt) and regional approach (Ritter)
Systematic approach: study one phenomenon worldwide, then build typologies and spatial patterns
Regional approach: divide the world into regions at different scales, then study all phenomena in one region
Dualism in geography: physical vs human; systematic vs regional
Branches based on systematic approach: physical geography (geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography)
Human geography branches: social/cultural, population and settlement, economic, historical, political geography
Biogeography branches: plant geography, zoo geography, ecology/ecosystem, environmental geography
Branches based on regional approach: regional studies/area studies, regional planning, regional development, regional analysis

Branches common to both: philosophy of geography (geographical thought, land and human interaction/human ecology), methods and techniques (cartography, quantitative techniques, field survey, geo-informatics: remote sensing, GIS, GPS)
Components of physical geography: lithosphere (geomorphology), atmosphere (climatology), hydrosphere (oceanography), biosphere (biogeography) and soils
Geomorphology: landforms, their evolution and processes
Climatology: structure of atmosphere, elements of weather, climate types and regions
Hydrology: realm of water, oceans, lakes, rivers; effect on life
Soil geography: soil formation, types, fertility status and distribution
Importance: landforms provide base for human activities; soils, water and climate as resources
Physical geography as basis for understanding natural resources and sustainable development
Exercise types: MCQs on approaches and branches; short answers on spatial synthesis; long answers on geography as an integrating discipline

chapters.title: Physical: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth

sections.name: 2.1 Early theories: origin of the earth

concepts.text: Nebular hypothesis of Immanuel Kant revised by mathematician Laplace (1796): planets from a cloud of slowly rotating material around a young sun
Chamberlain and Moulton (1900): wandering star approaching the sun, cigar-shaped material pulled out which condensed into planets
Sir James Jeans and Sir Harold Jeffrey supported the binary/wandering star idea
Otto Schmidt and Carl Weizascar (1950) revised nebular hypothesis: solar nebula of hydrogen, helium and dust; friction and collision formed a disk and planets by accretion

sections.name: 2.2 Modern theories: origin of the universe

concepts.text: Big Bang Theory (expanding universe hypothesis); Edwin Hubble (1920) evidence that universe is expanding (galaxies moving apart)
Analogy: balloon with marked points to show expansion of space between galaxies
Stage 1: all matter as a tiny ball (singular atom) of unimaginably small volume, infinite temperature and density
Stage 2: Big Bang about 13.7 billion years ago; violent expansion; energy converted to matter
Stage 3: within 300,000 years temperature dropped to 4500 K giving rise to atomic matter; universe became transparent
Hoyle's steady state concept (alternative view) and why the expanding universe view is now favoured
Uneven distribution of matter and energy in the early universe created density differences
Galaxy: huge collection of stars; diameter 80,000-150,000 light years
Nebula: large cloud of hydrogen gas from which a galaxy forms; localised clumps of gas grow into stars
Formation of stars dated to about 5-6 billion years ago
Light year as a measure of distance (distance light travels in one year, about 9.461 x 10^12 km)
Stage 1: stars as localised lumps of gas within a nebula; gravity forms a core and a rotating gas-dust disk
Stage 2: gas cloud condenses; matter around core forms small rounded objects - planetesimals
Stage 3: planetesimals collide and gravitationally accrete into a few large planets
Solar system: sun, 8 planets, satellites, asteroids, comets, dust; formed from solar nebula about 5-5.6 billion years ago, planets about 4.6 billion years ago
Terrestrial (inner) planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars - rocky, dense, small
Jovian (outer) planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune - gaseous giants
Reasons for difference: terrestrial planets formed close to the star where gases could not condense; solar wind removed gases near sun; small size gave weaker gravity
Table data type: planet distance from sun, density, radius and number of satellites
The Moon: giant impact theory (Big Splat) - body of Mars size hit the earth about 4.44 billion years ago; earlier view by Sir George Darwin (1838)
Earth initially barren, rocky, hot with thin atmosphere of hydrogen and helium
Layered structure from surface to centre; differences in density
Differentiation: lighter materials moved to surface, heavier ones sank towards centre during accretion
Formation of crust, mantle, outer core and inner core; moon-forming event heated the earth further
Three stages of evolution of the present atmosphere
Stage 1: loss of primordial atmosphere (hydrogen and helium) by solar winds
Stage 2: degassing - gases and water vapour released from the hot interior by volcanic eruptions
Early atmosphere dominated by water vapour, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and very little free oxygen
Condensation of water vapour, rainfall and formation of oceans within 500 million years; oceans are about 4 billion years old
Stage 3: photosynthesis by life in oceans added oxygen; oceans saturated with oxygen about 2,000 million years ago
Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater and oceans
Life began about 3.8 billion years ago as a chemical reaction producing complex organic molecules able to self-replicate
Evidence from fossils: blue-green algae (microscopic structures) in old rocks about 3,000 million years ago
Geological time scale (eons, eras, periods, epochs) and major life forms in each (Table: geological time scale)
Exercise types: MCQs on Big Bang/planets/moon; differentiate terrestrial and Jovian planets; describe stages of Big Bang; explain evolution of atmosphere; discuss early theories
Need to know the interior: landforms on the surface result from endogenic processes inside the earth
Radius of earth 6,370 km; deepest drilling (Kola, about 12 km) shows interior is not directly accessible

sections.name: 3.2 Sources of information about the interior

concepts.text: Direct sources: surface rocks from mining (e.g. gold mines of South Africa, 3-4 km deep)
Deep ocean drilling projects (Deep Ocean Drilling Project, Integrated Ocean Drilling Project) and Kola superdeep borehole (12 km)
Volcanic eruptions as a direct source: magma brought to the surface for laboratory analysis
Indirect sources: increase of temperature, pressure and density with depth
Meteors (meteorites) as indirect source - material similar to the earth's interior
Gravitation: gravity anomaly - difference between expected and observed gravity indicates distribution of mass
Magnetic surveys indicating distribution of magnetic materials in the crust
Seismic activity as the most important indirect source
Earthquake: shaking of the earth caused by release of energy generating waves in all directions
Release of energy along a fault; faults and sudden movement of rock blocks
Focus (hypocentre) and epicentre - point on surface directly above the focus where waves are first felt
Seismograph records waves reaching the surface

sections.name: 3.4 Earthquake waves: body waves and surface waves

concepts.text: Body waves generated at focus, travel through the interior; surface waves formed when body waves interact with surface rocks
P-waves (primary): fastest, longitudinal, travel through solid, liquid and gas; cause compression and rarefaction
S-waves (secondary): travel only through solids, transverse, vibrations perpendicular to direction of propagation; arrive later
Surface waves: last to reach the seismograph, most destructive, cause displacement of rocks and collapse of structures
Change in velocity and direction (reflection and refraction) of waves when passing through materials of different density

sections.name: 3.5 Propagation of earthquake waves and emergence of shadow zone

concepts.text: Diagram of how P and S waves cause vibrations in material
Shadow zone: area where waves are not recorded
Seismographs within 105 degrees from epicentre record both P and S waves
Beyond 145 degrees only P-waves recorded; zone between 105 and 145 degrees is shadow zone for both waves
S-wave shadow zone covers more than 40 percent of the earth's surface (beyond 105 degrees)
Shadow zone of S-waves as evidence that the outer core is liquid
Tectonic earthquakes: sliding of rocks along a fault plane - most common
Volcanic earthquakes: confined to areas of active volcanoes
Collapse earthquakes: roofs of underground mines collapse in mining areas
Explosion earthquakes: caused by explosion of chemical or nuclear devices
Reservoir induced earthquakes: occur in areas of large reservoirs
Magnitude scale (Richter scale): energy released, expressed in absolute numbers 0-10
Intensity scale (Mercalli scale): visible damage caused, range 1-12
Difference between magnitude and intensity of an earthquake
Hazards: ground shaking, differential ground settlement, land and mudslides, soil liquefaction
Ground lurching, avalanches, ground displacement, floods from dam and levee failures, fires
Structural collapse, falling objects, tsunami
Frequency of earthquake occurrences: higher-magnitude quakes rarer than low-magnitude ones
Case reference: earthquakes in India (e.g. Bhuj 2001) and worldwide

sections.name: 3.9 Structure of the earth: the crust

concepts.text: Crust: outermost solid part, brittle; thickness varies - oceanic crust about 5 km, continental about 30 km; up to 70 km under Himalayas
Density of crust about 3 g/cm3; oceanic crust made of basalt
Mantle extends from Moho discontinuity to 2,900 km depth
Asthenosphere: upper mantle up to 400 km, main source of magma, density higher than crust (3.4 g/cm3)
Lithosphere: crust plus uppermost solid mantle, thickness 10-200 km
Lower mantle is solid
Core-mantle boundary at 2,900 km depth (Gutenberg discontinuity)
Outer core liquid; inner core solid; density about 5 g/cm3 at boundary, about 13 g/cm3 at centre
Core made of very heavy material, mostly nickel and iron (nife)
Diagram type: label interior of the earth with layers, depths and discontinuities
Volcano: vent/opening through which gases, ash and molten rock (lava) erupt
Active volcano; magma vs lava; asthenosphere as source; materials: lava flows, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash, dust, gases (nitrogen, sulphur compounds, chlorine, hydrogen, argon)
Shield volcanoes: largest, mostly basalt, low viscosity lava, not steep (e.g. Hawaiian volcanoes); explosive if water enters vent
Composite volcanoes: cooler, viscous lava, explosive eruptions, layers of lava and pyroclastic material
Caldera: most explosive; volcano collapses on itself after eruption; indicates magma chamber close by
Flood basalt provinces: highly fluid lava over large areas (e.g. Deccan Traps in India)
Mid-ocean ridge volcanoes: extensive submarine ridge system with frequent eruptions
Intrusive forms: lava cooling inside the crust gives plutonic rocks; extrusive cooling gives volcanic rocks
Batholiths: large dome-shaped bodies of magma cooled deep in crust, granite; exposed after denudation
Lacoliths: large dome-shaped intrusive bodies with level base connected by a pipe-like conduit (e.g. Karnataka plateau granite domes)
Lapolith: saucer-shaped (concave) body; Phacolith: wavy mass at base of synclines or top of anticlines
Sills (thick horizontal bodies) and sheets (thin ones); dykes - vertical wall-like intrusions (common in western Maharashtra)
Exercise types: MCQs on layers and waves; differentiate P and S waves; explain shadow zone; indirect sources; volcanic landforms

chapters.title: Physical: Distribution of Oceans and Continents

concepts.text: Continents cover about 29 percent of the earth's surface, oceans the rest; positions changed over geological time
Early ideas: Abraham Ortelius (1596) on matching Atlantic coastlines; Antonio Pellegrini's map of joined continents
Alfred Wegener (German meteorologist, 1912) proposed continental drift theory
Pangaea (super continent) and Panthalassa (mega ocean)
About 200 million years ago Pangaea split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south)

sections.name: 4.3 Evidence in support of continental drift

concepts.text: Jig-saw fit of continents: Africa and South America shorelines; Bullard (1964) computer fit at 1,000-fathom line
Rocks of same age across oceans: 2,000 million years old belts of Brazil match western Africa; earliest marine deposits Jurassic
Tillite: sedimentary rock from glacial deposits; Gondwana system of India matches six southern landmasses - evidence of past glaciation
Placer deposits: gold of Ghana coast derived from Brazil plateau
Distribution of fossils: lemurs in India, Madagascar and Africa (Lemuria idea); Mesosaurus in South Africa and Brazil only
Force for drifting: pole-fleeing force (rotation, equatorial bulge) and tidal force (attraction of sun and moon); judged inadequate
Convectional current theory of Arthur Holmes (1930s): radioactive heat drives convection currents in the mantle
Mapping of the ocean floor after World War II: submerged mountain ranges, deep trenches, mid-ocean ridges
Ocean crust rocks much younger than continental rocks; equidistant rocks from ridge share age and composition
Three divisions of the ocean floor by depth and relief: continental margins, deep sea basins, mid-ocean ridges
Continental margins: shelf, slope, rise and deep oceanic trenches
Abyssal plains: extensive plains between continental margin and ridges where sediments accumulate
Mid-oceanic ridges: longest interconnected submarine mountain chain; central rift system, fractured plateau and flank zone; intense volcanism at crest
Line of earthquake and volcano dots along mid-oceanic ridges of Atlantic and Indian oceans
Second belt along the Alpine-Himalayan system and rim of the Pacific (Ring of Fire)
Shallow-focus quakes along mid-oceanic ridges; deep-seated quakes along Alpine-Himalayan belt and Pacific rim
Map work: Ring of Fire and Mid-Atlantic Ridge on world map
Palaeomagnetic observations: normal and reverse polarity stripes in rocks on either side of ridge
Rocks near ridge crest youngest; age increases away from crest
Ocean crust not older than 200 million years; continental rocks up to 3,200 million years
Thin sediments on ocean floor; deep earthquakes at trenches, shallow ones at ridges
Harry Hess (1961): magma rises at ridge, pushes crust apart; ocean floor spreads; old crust consumed at trenches (subduction)
Diagram: sea floor spreading
Theory proposed in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker and by Morgan
Tectonic/lithospheric plate: massive irregular slab of solid rock of continental and oceanic lithosphere moving over asthenosphere
Lithosphere thickness: 5-100 km under oceans, about 200 km in continental areas
Seven major plates: Antarctica, North American, South American, Pacific, India-Australia-New Zealand, Africa, Eurasia
Minor plates: Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji
Continents ride on plates; position of continents through geological past from palaeomagnetic data (Nagpur rocks for Indian position)
Map work: major and minor lithospheric plates of the world
Divergent boundaries (spreading sites): new crust generated as plates pull apart, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge
Convergent boundaries (subduction zones): crust destroyed as one plate dives under another
Three types of convergence: ocean-continent, ocean-ocean, continent-continent
Transform boundaries: plates slide horizontally past each other; crust neither created nor destroyed; transform faults perpendicular to ridges

sections.name: 4.10 Rates of plate movement and force for plate movement

concepts.text: Magnetic stripes used to calculate plate speeds
Arctic Ridge slowest (less than 2.5 cm/yr); East Pacific Rise near Easter Island fastest (over 15 cm/yr)
Mantle convection cells driven by radioactive decay and residual heat move the plates
Comparison: continental drift (continents move) vs plate tectonics (plates carrying continents and oceans move)
Indian plate includes peninsular India and Australian continental portions
Northern boundary: continent-continent convergence along Himalayas; eastern boundary along Rakinyoma mountains of Myanmar; western along Kirthar mountains of Pakistan and Makrana coast
India was a large island off Australian coast separated from Asia by Tethys sea till about 225 million years ago
Northward journey began about 200 million years ago; about 140 million years ago subcontinent near 50 degrees S
Deccan Traps lava outpouring about 60 million years ago when India was near equator
Collision with Asia about 40-50 million years ago; rapid uplift of Himalayas, still rising
Exercise types: evidence for drift; drift theory vs plate tectonics; post-drift discoveries; types of plate boundaries; position of India during Deccan Traps
Earth's surface shaped by endogenic forces (building) and exogenic forces (wearing down)
Geomorphic processes: endogenic and exogenic forces causing physical and chemical changes on earth materials
Geomorphic agent: mobile medium (running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves and currents) that removes, transports and deposits
Gravity as a directional force activating downslope movement; stresses create deformation
Energy from within the earth: radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, primordial heat (geothermal gradients)
Diastrophism: all processes that move, elevate or build up portions of crust
Orogeny: mountain building by severe folding along long belts
Epeirogeny: uplift or warping of large parts of crust
Earthquakes involving local minor movements; plate tectonics involving horizontal movements
Volcanism: movement of molten rock towards or onto the surface and formation of intrusive/extrusive forms
Energy from the atmosphere (sun) and gradients created by tectonic factors
Stress and shear stress; force applied per unit area breaking materials
Denudation: weathering, mass wasting/movements, erosion and transportation collectively
Exogenic processes depend on climate (temperature, precipitation), and on rock type and structure
Diagram: denudational processes and their driving forces
Climatic regimes and dominant exogenic processes vary across the earth
Weathering: action of elements of weather and climate on earth materials; in-situ or on-site process
Factors: geological, climatic, topographic, vegetative
Chemical weathering processes: solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction
Solution: dissolving of minerals in water or acids (e.g. calcium carbonate, salts)
Carbonation: reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate with minerals; carbonic acid dissolves limestone
Hydration: chemical addition of water causing volume increase (e.g. calcium sulphate to gypsum)
Oxidation and reduction: combination of minerals with oxygen (iron rusting, red colour); reduction in absence of oxygen
Physical/mechanical weathering: gravitational forces (overburden pressure, load), expansion forces due to temperature changes, crystal growth, animal activity, wetting and drying
Unloading and expansion: exfoliation domes and tors due to removal of overburden
Temperature changes and expansion: granular disintegration and exfoliation of surface layers
Freezing, thawing and frost wedging in cold climates
Salt weathering: salt crystallisation in pores, especially in dry areas
Biological activity and weathering: burrowing animals, plant roots, decaying organic matter, chelation
Special effects of weathering: exfoliation (flaking) and exfoliation domes
Significance of weathering: soil formation, enrichment of ores (iron, manganese, aluminium, copper), aids erosion and mass movement
Mass movement: movement of rock debris down slope under gravity; air, water or ice carry with debris but are not agents
Factors favouring: removal of support, increase in gradient, overloading, excess moisture, earthquakes, blasting, removal of vegetation
Three forms: heave (frost growth), flow and slide
Slow movements: creep (soil creep) and solifluction (water-saturated debris flow in cold climates)
Rapid movements: earthflow, mudflow and debris avalanche
Landslides: rapid perceptible movement of dry mass; slump, debris slide, rock slide, rock fall
Example: landslides in Himalayas vs Western Ghats (role of slopes and tectonics)
Erosion: acquisition and transportation of rock debris by geomorphic agents
Erosion vs weathering: erosion involves movement; weathering is in-situ
Kinetic energy of agents (running water, wind, glaciers, waves) drives erosion; abrasion by debris
Deposition as consequence of erosion when velocity and energy decrease
Running water dominant in humid regions; wind in hot dry deserts; glaciers in high latitudes/altitudes
Soil: collection of natural bodies on earth's surface containing living matter and supporting plants; dynamic medium
Process of soil formation: weathered material (regolith) colonised by bacteria, lichens, mosses; humus accumulation
Pedogenesis and soil profile (horizons)
Soil-forming factors: parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time
Parent material: passive control factor; in-situ (residual) or transported deposits
Topography: thin soils on steep slopes, thick on flat uplands; aspect effect
Climate: moisture, precipitation, evaporation, temperature; eluviation and illuviation; leaching, calcification, salinisation in dry climates
Biological activity: organic matter, humus, nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium), bacterial activity higher in humid tropics
Time: mature soil profile development; young vs mature soils
Exercise types: differentiate weathering and erosion; endogenic vs exogenic; explain chemical weathering processes; soil-forming factors; significance of weathering
Weathered material eroded, transported and deposited by agents creates landforms
Landform: small to medium tract of earth surface; landscape: large tract of related landforms
Each landform has its own shape, size, materials and history; evolution through stages: youth, maturity and old age
Two aspects of landform evolution: stages of development and the processes of agents
Running water as the most important agent in humid regions: overland (sheet) flow and linear flow (streams, rivers)
Youth: few streams, V-shaped valleys, poor integration, waterfalls and rapids, shallow valleys
Maturity: plenty of streams, good integration, deep V-shaped valleys, wide floodplains, meanders
Old age: smaller tributaries, gentle gradients, lakes, swamps, marshes, extensive floodplains
Peneplain (almost plain) with low resistant remnants called monadnocks
Valleys from rills to gullies; V-shaped valley, gorge (steep sides, same width at top and bottom) and canyon (step-like sides, wider at top)
Example: Kaveri valley gorge near Hogenekal; Grand Canyon of Colorado River
Potholes: circular depressions by abrasion of rock fragments; plunge pools at foot of waterfalls
Incised or entrenched meanders: deep meandering gorges cut in hard rock; indicate uplift
River terraces: old valley floor levels; paired and unpaired terraces; causes - receding water, hydrological changes, tectonic uplift, sea-level change
Alluvial fans: cone-shaped deposits at the foot of slopes where streams enter plains
Deltas: deposits at river mouths, layered and stratified, distributaries (e.g. Krishna delta)
Floodplains: active floodplain (riverbed level) and inactive floodplain; delta plain
Natural levees: low linear ridges along banks deposited during floods
Point bars (meander bars): deposits on convex side of meanders
Meanders: loop-like channel pattern due to gentle gradient, unconsolidated alluvium, Coriolis force; meander is not a landform but a channel pattern
Oxbow lakes (cut-off lakes) formed when meander loops are cut off
Difference between natural levees and point bars
Groundwater work effective in limestone/dolomite areas rich in calcium carbonate; process mainly solution and precipitation
Karst topography named after the Karst region of the Balkans (Adriatic Sea)
Erosional landforms: swallow holes (small funnel-shaped openings) and sinkholes
Solution sinks vs collapse sinks (dolines)
Valley sinks or uvalas: long narrow trenches formed by merging sinkholes
Lapies: irregular grooves and ridges on limestone surface; limestone pavements
Caves: formed in alternating beds of rocks; tunnels; caves with open ends
Depositional landforms: stalactites (hanging icicles from roof), stalagmites (rising from floor), pillars/columns
Why underground drainage dominates surface flow in limestone areas
Glacier: mass of ice moving as sheets over land (continental/piedmont glaciers) or as linear flows in valleys (mountain/valley glaciers)
Glacial erosion by friction of ice; plucking and abrasion
Example box: Gangotri glacier, Gaumukh snout, Bhagirathi and Alaknanda join at Deoprayag
Cirque: deep bowl-shaped depression at head of glacial valley; tarn lake inside
Horns and serrated ridges (aretes): sharp peaks formed by headward erosion of cirques (e.g. Matterhorn, Everest)
Glacial valleys/troughs: U-shaped valleys, hanging valleys; fjords (very deep valleys filled with sea water)
Glacial till: unsorted coarse and fine debris; outwash deposits: sorted and stratified by meltwater
Moraines: terminal, lateral, medial and ground moraines
Eskers: sinuous ridges of coarse material deposited by meltwater streams under glaciers
Outwash plains: broad flat alluvial fans of glacio-fluvial deposits
Drumlins: smooth oval ridge-like features of till; stoss end and tail indicate direction of ice movement
Differences: glacial valley vs river valley; till vs alluvium; outwash plain vs alluvial plain
Coastal processes most dynamic; breaking waves, storm waves and tsunamis cause changes
Two types of coasts: high rocky (submerged) coasts and low smooth gently sloping sedimentary (emerged) coasts
High rocky coasts: erosion dominant; cliffs, irregular coastline; west coast of India example
Low sedimentary coasts: deposition dominant; lagoons, deltas, marshes; east coast of India example
Erosional landforms: sea cliffs, wave-cut platforms/terraces, sea caves, sea stacks
Depositional landforms: beaches (sandy and shingle), sand dunes
Offshore bars, barrier bars and spits; lagoons formed behind bars; spit in Godavari delta
Bars, barriers and mangroves as buffers against storm and tsunami waves
Differences between high rocky and low sedimentary coasts
Hot deserts: wind as dominant agent; also sheet floods and rain contribute
Wind erosion processes: deflation, abrasion and impact
Pediments: gently inclined rocky floors at foot of mountains formed by lateral erosion; pediplains
Inselbergs: remnants of mountains on pediplain
Playas: shallow lakes in basins with salt deposits; alkali flats
Deflation hollows and caves (blow outs)
Mushroom rocks, table and pedestal rocks shaped by wind abrasion
Sand dunes: barchans (crescent-shaped, horns away from wind), parabolic dunes, seifs, longitudinal and transverse dunes
Exercise types: identify landform by description; stages of river valleys; behaviour of limestone in humid vs arid climates; glacial and desert landform explanations

chapters.title: Physical: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere

concepts.text: Atmosphere: mixture of gases enveloping the earth; essential for life; 99 percent of mass within 32 km
Air as a mixture of gases, water vapour and dust particles; density falls with height
Permanent gases: nitrogen (78.08 percent) and oxygen (20.95 percent), argon, carbon dioxide and others
Table data: percentage volume of gases in dry air (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, neon, helium, krypton, xenon, hydrogen)
Oxygen negligible at 120 km; carbon dioxide and water vapour up to 90 km
Carbon dioxide: transparent to incoming solar radiation, opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation - greenhouse effect
Rising carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels raises air temperature
Ozone: located 10-50 km above surface; filters ultraviolet rays

sections.name: 7.3 Composition: water vapour and dust particles

concepts.text: Water vapour: variable gas, up to 4 percent in warm wet tropics, less than 1 percent in cold dry regions; decreases from equator to poles
Water vapour absorbs insolation and terrestrial radiation (acts like a blanket), and keeps earth neither too hot nor too cold; contributes to stability/instability
Dust particles: sea salt, fine soil, smoke-soot, ash, pollen, meteor dust; concentrated in subtropical and temperate regions
Dust and salt particles as hygroscopic nuclei for cloud condensation
Five layers by temperature: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere
Troposphere: lowest layer, average height 13 km; about 8 km at poles and 18 km at equator; contains dust and water vapour; all weather changes
Normal lapse rate in troposphere: temperature falls 1 degree C per 165 m
Tropopause: transition zone; temperature about -80 degrees C over equator and -45 degrees C over poles
Stratosphere: up to 50 km; contains ozone layer that absorbs UV radiation
Mesosphere: 50-80 km; temperature falls to -100 degrees C at 80 km; mesopause
Ionosphere/thermosphere: 80-400 km, electrically charged particles (ions) reflect radio waves; temperature increases with height
Exosphere: uppermost layer, very thin, gases gradually merge with outer space
Diagram type: draw and label structure of atmosphere with heights and temperature trend
Main elements: temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, clouds and precipitation (studied in later chapters)
Exercise types: MCQs on gas percentages and layers; importance of water vapour and dust; why troposphere is most important; ozone role

chapters.title: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

concepts.text: Insolation: incoming solar radiation received in short wavelengths; earth intercepts a small part
Average insolation at top of atmosphere about 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute (solar constant idea)
Aphelion (4 July, farthest, 152 million km) and perihelion (3 January, nearest, 147 million km); slightly more insolation on 3 January but masked by land-sea distribution

sections.name: 8.2 Variability of insolation at the surface

concepts.text: Factors: rotation of the earth on its axis, angle of inclination of sun's rays, length of day, transparency of atmosphere, configuration of land (aspect)
Earth's axis inclined at 66.5 degrees to the plane of orbit affects insolation at latitudes
Angle of rays: slant rays cover larger area and pass through more atmosphere so give less energy
Passage of solar radiation through atmosphere: scattering (blue sky, red sunrise and sunset), absorption by water vapour, ozone
Spatial distribution: maximum in subtropical deserts (least cloudiness); equator gets less than tropics; more over continents than oceans; winter middle and high latitudes get less

sections.name: 8.3 Heating and cooling of the atmosphere

concepts.text: Earth heated by insolation transmits heat to atmosphere in long wave form
Conduction: transfer of heat between bodies in contact; heats lower layers
Convection: vertical transfer of heat by rising heated air; confined to troposphere
Advection: horizontal transfer of heat by wind; more important in middle latitudes; loo winds in northern India as example
Earth after heating radiates energy in long wave form to the atmosphere
Atmosphere heated indirectly by terrestrial radiation; greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide) absorb long waves
Atmosphere radiates heat to space, maintaining constant temperature over time

sections.name: 8.5 Heat budget of the planet earth

concepts.text: Earth neither warms nor cools on average: balance of incoming insolation and outgoing radiation
Of 100 units of insolation: 35 reflected (27 from clouds top, 2 from snow and ice) - albedo; 6 scattered to space
Remaining 65 units absorbed: 14 within atmosphere, 51 by earth's surface
Earth radiates 51 units: 17 directly to space, 34 absorbed by atmosphere (6 directly, 9 convection/turbulence, 19 latent heat of condensation)
Atmosphere radiates 48 units (14 + 34) back to space; total 17 + 48 = 65 units balances absorbed
Diagram: heat budget of the earth (flow chart with units)
Albedo: amount of reflected radiation

sections.name: 8.6 Variation in the net heat budget at the earth's surface

concepts.text: Surplus of net radiation between 40 degrees N and 40 degrees S; deficit near poles
Transfer of surplus heat from tropics to poles by winds and ocean currents prevents tropics from overheating and poles from freezing
Graph type: latitudinal variation in net radiation balance
Temperature: measurement in degrees of how hot or cold; heat vs temperature
Latitude: insolation depends on latitude
Altitude: temperature decreases with height; normal lapse rate 6.5 degrees C per 1,000 m
Distance from the sea: moderating influence of sea; land-sea breezes; continentality
Air mass and ocean currents: warm and cold currents and air masses influence coastal temperature
Isotherms: lines joining places of equal temperature; generally parallel to latitude
January distribution: isotherms deviate north over oceans and south over continents in northern hemisphere; Siberian plain very cold
Effect of Gulf Stream and North Atlantic drift in January isotherms
July distribution: isotherms generally parallel; equatorial oceans above 27 degrees C; over 30 degrees C over subtropical continents of Asia
Southern hemisphere isotherms more regular due to larger oceans; Range of temperature between January and July highest in north-eastern Eurasia (over 60 degrees C)
Map reading: interpret January and July isotherm maps
Normal lapse rate vs inversion where temperature increases with height
Ideal conditions: long winter nights, clear skies, calm still air
Surface inversion promotes stability; smoke and dust collect near ground - dense fog in winter mornings
Air drainage: cold dense air flows down slopes and collects in valleys; frost in valley bottoms - plants protected on slopes
Plank's law: hotter body radiates more energy at shorter wavelengths
Specific heat: energy needed to raise temperature of one gram by 1 degree C
Exercise types: heat budget explanation; factors controlling temperature; why subtropics get more insolation than equator; isotherm patterns; inversion conditions

chapters.title: Physical: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems

concepts.text: Air pressure: weight of a column of air per unit area from mean sea level to top of atmosphere, measured in millibars
Mean sea level pressure 1,013.2 mb; measured by mercury barometer or aneroid barometer
Vertical variation: pressure decreases about 1 mb per 10 m rise
Vertical pressure gradient force balanced by gravity, so strong upward winds do not occur
Horizontal distribution: isobars on maps reduced to sea level; low pressure and high pressure systems
Close isobars indicate steep pressure gradient; widely spaced show gentle gradient

sections.name: 9.2 World distribution of sea level pressure

concepts.text: Equatorial low (equatorial trough) near equator
Subtropical highs around 30 degrees N and S
Subpolar lows around 60 degrees N and S; polar highs near poles
Seasonal shift of pressure belts with apparent movement of the sun
Map reading: world pressure in January and July

sections.name: 9.3 Forces affecting the velocity and direction of wind

concepts.text: Wind: air moving from high to low pressure
Pressure gradient force: rate of change of pressure with distance
Frictional force: greatest at surface, extends up to 1-3 km
Coriolis force: due to rotation, deflects winds to right in northern hemisphere and left in southern; maximum at poles, absent at equator; described by Coriolis (1844)
Pressure and wind: geostrophic wind - balance of pressure gradient and Coriolis force in upper atmosphere (2-3 km above)
Cyclonic circulation (around low) and anticyclonic circulation (around high); directions in both hemispheres (Table: pattern of wind direction in cyclones and anticyclones)
Convergence at low leads to rising air; divergence at high leads to subsidence
Pattern of planetary winds depends on latitudinal heating, emergence of pressure belts, migration of belts with sun, land-sea distribution and earth's rotation
Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ): convergence of trade winds; ascending air at equator
Hadley cell (tropical cell): rising at ITCZ and sinking at subtropics, returning as easterly trade winds
Ferrel cell in middle latitudes: westerlies at surface
Polar cell: cold dense air subsiding at poles, blowing as polar easterlies
Three-cell model transfers heat from lower to higher latitudes; diagram of simplified general circulation
General atmospheric circulation and its effects on oceans: El Nino, Southern Oscillation (ENSO), walker circulation
El Nino: warm water off Peru replaces cold Peruvian current; effects on weather worldwide and Indian monsoon
Seasonal winds: shift of wind belts creates monsoon in South-east Asia
Land and sea breezes: diurnal changes in heating of land and sea
Mountain and valley winds: valley breeze by day, mountain (katabatic) wind at night
Local winds examples: cold air drainage; warm winds on leeward side (Foehn in Alps, Chinook in Rockies)
Air mass: large body of air with uniform temperature and humidity acquired from source region
Source regions: warm tropical and subtropical oceans, subtropical hot deserts, cold high-latitude oceans, snow-covered continents, Arctic/Antarctic
Types: maritime tropical (mT), continental tropical (cT), maritime polar (mP), continental polar (cP), continental arctic (cA)
Front: boundary zone where two air masses of different characteristics meet; frontogenesis
Four types: cold front, warm front, stationary front and occluded front
Cold front: cold air moves towards warm air; warm front: warm air moves over cold air
Stationary front when front is stationary; occluded front when cold air mass overtakes warm air mass
Fronts occur in middle latitudes; steep gradients; weather changes along fronts
Develop in mid and high latitudes beyond tropics, along polar front
Formation: warm and cold air masses meet; wave forms; warm sector between warm front and cold front; occlusion
Differences from tropical cyclones: clear frontal system, larger area, origin over land and sea, move west to east, weaker winds
Violent storms originating over tropical oceans moving to coasts; called cyclones (Indian Ocean), hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (western Pacific), willy-willies (western Australia)
Conditions: large sea surface with temperature over 27 degrees C, presence of Coriolis force, small variation in vertical wind speed, pre-existing weak low pressure, upper divergence
Energy from latent heat of condensation; dissipates on landfall
Structure: eye (calm centre with subsiding air), eye wall (strongest winds, heavy rain), rain bands
Diameter 150-250 km in Bay of Bengal/Arabian Sea; landfall and storm surge
Diagram: vertical section of tropical cyclone
Thunderstorms: brief intense storms with thunder, lightning, heavy rain/hail from cumulonimbus clouds; caused by intense convection on hot humid days
Tornadoes: violent spiralling descending air with very low pressure at centre in middle latitudes; water spouts over sea
Exercise types: forces affecting winds; general circulation diagram; ITCZ; differences between tropical and extra-tropical cyclones; air masses and fronts
Water vapour in air ranges 0-4 percent by volume; water cycle among atmosphere, oceans and continents
Humidity: water vapour present in air
Absolute humidity: actual amount of water vapour per unit volume of air (grams per cubic metre)
Relative humidity: percentage of moisture present compared with full capacity at given temperature
Saturated air; dew point - temperature at which saturation occurs
Relative humidity greater over oceans, least over continents
Evaporation: water changes to vapour; latent heat of vaporisation; depends on temperature, unsaturation, air movement
Condensation: transformation of vapour into water by loss of heat
Condensation occurs when temperature drops to dew point, volume of air changes, or contact with cold object
Conditions favourable for condensation: cooling of air, hygroscopic condensation nuclei
Sublimation: vapour directly to solid (ice) when dew point below freezing
Dew: moisture deposited as droplets on cold surfaces; dew point above freezing; clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, cold long nights
Frost: condensation on cold surfaces when dew point below freezing; white frost
Fog and mist: cloud at or near ground; smog in urban/industrial areas; mist contains more moisture than fog
Clouds: mass of minute water droplets or ice crystals formed by condensation at considerable elevation
Classification by height, expanse, density and transparency
Cirrus: high altitudes 8,000-12,000 m, thin detached feathery; white
Cumulus: cotton wool-like, 4,000-7,000 m, flat base
Stratus: layered clouds covering large portions of sky
Nimbus: black or dark grey, low or middle level, close to surface, extremely dense; thick vapour masses

Combination forms: high clouds (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus), middle clouds (altostratus, altocumulus), low clouds (stratocumulus, nimbostratus) and vertical development clouds (cumulus, cumulonimbus)
Precipitation: release of moisture after continuous condensation when droplets grow heavy
Forms: rainfall (water), snowfall (ice flakes below 0 degrees C)
Sleet: frozen raindrops and refrozen melted snow
Hailstones: rain drops freezing into small rounded ice pellets passing through cold layers; several concentric layers
Classified by origin: convectional, orographic and cyclonic (frontal)
Convectional rain: heated air rises, cools and forms cumulus clouds; heavy short-duration rain with thunder in equatorial regions and summer afternoons
Orographic (relief) rain: saturated air mass rises over a mountain; windward side rainy, leeward rain-shadow area
Cyclonic rain: associated with cyclones and fronts (explained in chapter on atmospheric circulation)
Diagram: orographic rainfall and rain-shadow
Rainfall decreases from equator to poles
Coastal areas get more rain than continental interiors; more rain over oceans than land
Between 35 and 40 degrees N and S rain heavier on eastern coasts; westerly belt (45-65 degrees) brings rain to western margins
Mountains receive more on windward side
Rainfall regimes: over 200 cm (equatorial belt, windward slopes, monsoon coasts), 100-200 cm, 50-100 cm, less than 50 cm (deserts, interiors)
Seasonal distribution: equatorial belt rain throughout year; monsoon lands summer rain; Mediterranean lands winter rain
Exercise types: absolute vs relative humidity; forms of condensation; types of rainfall with diagrams; world rainfall distribution map reading

chapters.title: Physical: World Climate and Climate Change

concepts.text: Three approaches to climate classification: empirical (observed data on temperature and precipitation), genetic (causes) and applied (specific purposes)
Koeppen's empirical classification based on mean annual and mean monthly temperature and precipitation, related to vegetation distribution
Koeppen used capital letters for major groups: A, C, D and E humid; B dry
Small letters for seasons of dryness: f (no dry season), m (monsoon), w (winter dry), s (summer dry)
Letters S (steppe) and W (desert); additional letters for temperature (a, b, c, d) and h, k for hot/cold dry climates
Tables: climatic groups according to Koeppen (A, B, C, D, E, H) and climatic types with characteristics
Between Tropic of Cancer and Capricorn; sun overhead, ITCZ; hot and humid; small annual temperature range, high rainfall
Tropical wet climate (Af): near equator - Amazon basin, western equatorial Africa, East Indies islands; rain every month, thunder showers in afternoon
Tropical monsoon climate (Am): Indian subcontinent, north-east South America, northern Australia; heavy summer rain, dry winter
Tropical wet and dry climate (Aw): north and south of Af; savanna; dry season severe
Very low rainfall inadequate for plant growth; large area of planet from 15-60 degrees N and S
Subtropical steppe (BSh) and subtropical desert (BWh) between 15-35 degrees; mid-latitude steppe (BSk) and desert (BWk) between 35-60 degrees
Low rainfall due to subsidence and inversion of temperature; fog in coastal deserts with cold currents
High diurnal and annual temperature ranges; maximum summer temperature very high (e.g. Al Aziziyah, Libya 58 degrees C)
Extend from 30-50 degrees latitude mainly on eastern and western margins of continents; warm summers, mild winters
Humid subtropical (Cwa): poleward of Tropic of Cancer and Capricorn in North Indian plains and South China interior; dry winter
Mediterranean (Cs): around Mediterranean Sea, west coasts of continents 30-40 degrees - central California, central Chile, SE and SW Australia; hot dry summer, mild wet winter
Humid subtropical (Cfa): eastern parts of continents in subtropics - USA, southern Japan, NE Argentina, coastal south Africa, eastern Australia; rainfall throughout year

Marine west coast (Cfb): poleward of Mediterranean on west coasts - NW Europe, west coast of North America, north California, southern Chile, SE Australia, New Zealand; moderate temperature, rain all year

sections.name: 11.5 Group D: cold snow forest climates

concepts.text: Found in large continental areas in northern hemisphere between 40-70 degrees: Eurasia and North America
Cold climate with humid winters (Df): poleward of marine west coast and mid-latitude steppe; severe winters, short summers
Cold climate with dry winters (Dw): mainly over NE Asia; pronounced winter anticyclone; very low winter temperature (e.g. Verkhoyansk)
Poleward beyond 70 degrees latitude
Tundra (ET): named after vegetation type of mosses, lichens and flowering plants; permafrost; long daylight in summer
Ice cap (ETF): over interior Greenland and Antarctica; below freezing; heavy snow; ice sheets
Highland climates (H): governed by topography; altitudinal zones
Climate changes over geological time (Pleistocene glacial and inter-glacial periods); evidence from glaciers, sediments, tree rings
Climate in recent past: dry spells in Rajasthan (Harappan period), 8000 BC to 3000 BC warm, Little Ice Age in Europe (1550-1850), warming in 20th century
Natural causes: astronomical (sunspot activity), Milankovitch oscillations (eccentricity, wobble, tilt), volcanism (aerosols lower temperature)
Anthropogenic causes: rise in greenhouse gases
Greenhouse effect: atmosphere acts like a greenhouse - transparent to insolation, opaque to outgoing long-wave radiation
Greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), methane, nitrous oxide, ozone; their potential and lifetime
Sources: fossil fuels, deforestation (CO2), CFCs from refrigeration and aerosols, methane from wetlands and paddy, nitrous oxide
Ozone depletion by CFCs; ozone hole over Antarctica
Kyoto Protocol (1997, effective 2005) - industrialised nations to reduce emissions; later international efforts
Effects: rise in global temperature by about 0.7 degrees C in past century, sea-level rise, melting ice caps, impact on agriculture and coastal settlements
Exercise types: MCQs on Koeppen letters and climate types; tundra vs Mediterranean characteristics; causes of climate change; greenhouse gases and global warming effects
Earth as the blue planet; about 71 percent of surface covered by water
Hydrological cycle: circulation of water among hydrosphere, atmosphere, lithosphere and biosphere in liquid, solid and gas forms
About 71 percent of planetary water in oceans; remainder in glaciers, ice caps, groundwater, lakes, soil moisture, atmosphere, streams and life
Table data: water on earth surface (oceans 97.3 percent, ice caps and glaciers 2.0 percent, groundwater 0.68 percent etc.)
Components and processes: evaporation, evapotranspiration, sublimation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration, groundwater flow
Diagram: hydrological cycle
Rising demand for water and water stress; need to manage water sustainably

sections.name: 12.2 Relief of the ocean floor: divisions

concepts.text: Oceans confined to great depressions of the earth's outer layer: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans
Ocean floor divided into four major divisions: continental shelf, continental slope, deep sea plain and oceanic deeps
Continental shelf: extended margin of continent bounded by shelf break; average width 80 km; depth 30-600 m; gradient 1 degree or less; rich sediments and fossil fuels; e.g. Siberian shelf (largest)
Continental slope: connects shelf and ocean basins; gradient 2-5 degrees; depth 200-3,000 m; canyons and trenches
Deep sea plain (abyssal plain): gently sloping, flattest and smoothest; depth 3,000-6,000 m; fine-grained sediments

Oceanic deeps or trenches: deepest parts, long narrow basins, 3-5 km deeper than ocean floor; near continents and island arcs; associated with volcanoes and earthquakes; 57 deeps explored (32 in Pacific)
Mid-oceanic ridges: two chains of mountains separated by depression; peaks emerge as islands (e.g. Iceland in Mid-Atlantic Ridge)
Seamount: mountain with pointed summit rising from sea floor not reaching surface; volcanic; e.g. Emperor seamount
Submarine canyons: deep valleys cutting across shelves and slopes; e.g. Hudson canyon
Guyots: flat-topped seamounts; gradual subsidence
Atoll: low islands of coral reefs surrounding a central depression (lagoon)
Diagram: relief of ocean floor
Ocean water heated by solar energy; heated and cooled slower than land
Factors affecting temperature distribution: latitude, unequal distribution of land and water, prevailing wind, ocean currents
Northern hemisphere oceans warmer due to more land contact; offshore winds cause upwelling of cold water
Horizontal distribution: average surface temperature about 27 degrees C; decreases from equator to poles at 0.5 degrees C per latitude
Vertical distribution: temperature falls with depth; three-layer system
First layer: warm top 500 m (20-25 degrees C) in tropics; second layer: thermocline (500-1,000 m) with rapid temperature drop; third layer: very cold deep layer near 0 degrees C
Arctic and Antarctic: surface temperature close to 0 degrees C with little change with depth (one layer)
Highest temperature not at equator but slightly north of it; enclosed seas warmer
Salinity: total amount of dissolved salts in sea water, expressed as parts per thousand (o/oo); 24.7 o/oo used to delimit brackish water
Table data: dissolved salts in sea water - sodium chloride, magnesium chloride, magnesium sulphate, calcium sulphate, potassium sulphate etc.
Factors: evaporation and precipitation; fresh water from rivers and melting ice in polar regions; wind; ocean currents
Horizontal distribution: normal open ocean 33-37 o/oo; Red Sea up to 41 o/oo; Baltic Sea low (dilution); Mediterranean high (evaporation); Dead Sea, Great Salt Lake, Lake Van very saline
North Atlantic high salinity (36-37 o/oo between 15-20 degrees N); Arabian Sea higher than Bay of Bengal (Ganga influx)
Vertical distribution: salinity changes with depth; halocline - zone of sharp salinity change
Higher salinity water denser and sinks; salinity linked to density
Map reading: surface salinity of world oceans
Exercise types: hydrological cycle explanation; ocean floor relief features with diagram; factors and distribution of temperature and salinity
Ocean water dynamic: physical characteristics (temperature, salinity, density) and external forces (sun, moon, winds)
Horizontal motion: ocean currents and waves; vertical motion: tides and upwelling/sinking
Currents: continuous flow of huge water in a definite direction; waves: horizontal motion of water surface
Waves are energy, not water, moving across ocean surface; water particles move in small circles
Wind provides energy; waves travel and break on shores; largest waves in open ocean
Wave grows with wind speed, duration and fetch (distance of open water)
Characteristics: wave crest and trough, wave height, wave amplitude, wave period, wavelength, wave speed, wave frequency
Wave breaking: wave slows in shallow water, steepens and breaks (surf)
Diagram: motion of waves and water molecules
Tides: periodical rise and fall of sea level once or twice a day due to attraction of sun and moon
Surges: movement of water caused by meteorological effects (winds, atmospheric pressure) - not tides
Cause: gravitational pull of moon (more important) and sun, and centrifugal force
Tidal bulges on side facing the moon and the opposite side; tidal ranges higher where shelves are wide
Bay of Fundy (Canada) has highest tides (about 15-16 m); tidal bores in estuaries
Based on frequency: semi-diurnal tide (two highs and two lows daily, most common), diurnal tide (one high and one low), mixed tide (variations in height)
Based on sun, moon and earth positions: spring tides (sun, moon, earth in a line - full and new moon), neap tides (sun and moon at right angles, seven days after spring)
Perigee (moon nearest, higher tidal range) and apogee (moon farthest); perihelion (earth nearest sun, early January) and aphelion (early July)
Ebb (low tide) and flood (high tide); time between high tides about 12 hours 25 minutes
Importance of tides: navigation (tidal ports, e.g. Kolkata), fishing, desilting of harbours, tidal energy generation (e.g. Bay of Fundy, Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat, Sundarbans in India)
Ocean currents: river-like flow of water in a definite path and direction
Primary forces: heating by solar energy, wind, gravity and Coriolis force
Secondary forces: differences in water density due to temperature and salinity; cold dense water sinks at poles
Types by depth: surface currents (about 10 percent of ocean water, upper 400 m) and deep water currents (90 percent, thermohaline circulation)
Types by temperature: cold currents (from high to low latitudes, west coasts in low and middle latitudes) and warm currents (from low to high latitudes, east coasts in low and middle latitudes)
Drift: current flowing slowly; stream: current moving fast
Influenced by prevailing winds and Coriolis force; gyres - large circular currents in major ocean basins
Clockwise circulation in northern hemisphere, anti-clockwise in southern
Warm currents: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil, Agulhas, Alaska, North Atlantic drift, East Australian
Cold currents: Labrador, Canaries, California, Humboldt (Peru), Benguela, Falkland, West Australian, Oyashio
Map work: world ocean currents (warm and cold)
Effects of ocean currents: desert formation on west coasts with cold currents; moderate climate on west coasts of middle/high latitudes with warm currents
Mixing of warm and cold currents creates rich fishing grounds (e.g. Grand Banks near Newfoundland, Hokkaido)
Exercise types: types of tides; importance of tides; factors of ocean currents; warm vs cold currents effects; wave characteristics
Biodiversity: number and variety of organisms in a region; variability among plants, animals and microorganisms, genes and ecosystems
Biodiversity as outcome of 2.5-3.5 billion years of evolution; species turnover
Biodiversity richest in tropics; species are not evenly distributed
Genetic diversity: variation of genes within species; basis of species' adaptability; e.g. different human races
Species diversity: variety of species; species richness; hotspots of biodiversity
Ecosystem diversity: variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes; boundaries of ecosystems are difficult to delimit
Ecological role: species capture and store energy, decompose organic matter, cycle water and nutrients, fix gases, regulate climate
Economic role: food crops, livestock, forestry, fish, medicinal resources; raw materials for industries (dyes, fibres, fragrances, oils, rubber, timber)
Scientific role: each species gives clues about evolution; understanding of how life functions and role of each species
Ethical value: all species have a right to exist; human responsibility
Human population growth increases consumption and destroys habitats
Tropical regions with only one-fourth area hold three-fourths of human population; overexploitation and deforestation
Natural calamities: earthquakes, floods, volcanic eruptions, forest fires, droughts damage flora and fauna
Pesticides and pollutants (hydrocarbons, heavy metals) harm vulnerable species
Exotic species introduced into habitats disturb natural communities
Poaching and illegal trade (tusks, horns, hides, skins)
International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN) classifies threatened species
Endangered species: in danger of extinction; listed in Red Data Book
Vulnerable species: likely to become endangered if threats continue
Rare species: small world populations
Other categories: extinct and not sighted in last 50 years; insufficiently known species
Need for conservation: survival and welfare of humans; concept of sustainable use
Strategies (World Conservation Strategy): conserve species, prevent extinction, protect habitats, list wild species, establish protected areas
Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 in India; protected areas - national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves
Convention on Biological Diversity (Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro 1992); India a signatory
Megadiversity centres: 12 countries with high diversity including India, Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, DR Congo, Madagascar, China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia
Hotspots of biodiversity: areas with high species richness and endemism; criteria (Norman Myers); hotspots including Eastern Himalaya, Western Ghats
Map work: ecological hotspots - Eastern Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indonesia, Eastern Madagascar, Upper Guinean forests, Atlantic forest, Tropical Andes
Exercise types: levels of biodiversity; reasons for loss; IUCN categories; role of biodiversity; conservation methods; hotspots
India's mainland extends from Kashmir to Kanniyakumari and from Arunachal Pradesh to Gujarat
Territorial limit extends to 12 nautical miles (about 21.9 km) into the sea
Latitudinal extent of mainland: 8 degrees 4' N to 37 degrees 6' N; longitudinal extent 68 degrees 7' E to 97 degrees 25' E
North-south extent about 3,214 km and east-west about 2,933 km
Tropic of Cancer (23 degrees 30' N) divides India almost into two equal halves: tropical south and subtropical north
Implication of latitudinal extent: day length variation; longitudinal extent: about two hours time difference between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh
Standard meridian of India: 82 degrees 30' E passing through Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh)
IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time
Why countries choose a standard meridian (multiples of 7 degrees 30')
Activity type: compute local time difference between places from longitude
Area 3.28 million sq km; about 2.4 percent of world land area; seventh largest country
Physical diversity due to size: Himalayas in north, Indian Ocean in south, desert in west, forested hills in east
Mainland coastline 6,100 km; total coastline with islands (Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep) 7,517 km
Land boundaries: young fold mountains in north-west, north and north-east; peninsula tapering south of 22 degrees N into Indian Ocean
India in south-central Asia bordering Indian Ocean (Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal); strategic central position in Indian Ocean
Land neighbours: Pakistan and Afghanistan in north-west, China (Tibet), Nepal, Bhutan in north, Myanmar and Bangladesh in east
Island neighbours: Sri Lanka (separated by Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar) and Maldives (south of Lakshadweep)
Map work: latitudinal and longitudinal extent, Standard Meridian, Tropic of Cancer, Kanyakumari; India's neighbours on outline map
Exercise types: MCQs on extent and neighbours; significance of Standard Meridian; why Tropic of Cancer matters; India's strategic location
Earth about 4,600 million years old; evolution through endogenic and exogenic forces
Indian plate was south of equator; northward movement and collision with Eurasian plate formed Himalayas
India divided into three geological divisions based on structure and formation: Peninsular block, Himalayas and other Peninsular mountains, Indo-Ganga-Brahmaputra plain
Boundary: irregular line from Kachchh along western flank of Aravali, near Delhi, parallel to Yamuna and Ganga to Rajmahal hills and Ganga delta; Karbi Anglong and Meghalaya plateau in north-east
Made of ancient gneisses and granites; stable since Cambrian; rigid block
Western coast submerged under sea; parts affected by faulting
Relict and residual mountains: Aravali, Nallamala, Javadi, Veliconda, Palkonda, Mahendragiri hills
Shallow graded river valleys with low gradients; rift valleys of Narmada and Tapi (and Mahanadi)

sections.name: 16.3 The Himalayas and other Peninsular mountains

concepts.text: Young, weak and flexible geological structure; still subject to tectonic forces - faulting, folding, thrusting
Tectonic origin; youthful topography with gorges, V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls
Diagram/section: Himalayan mountains
Plains formed by Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; originally a geo-synclinal depression formed during third phase of Himalayan orogeny (about 64 million years ago)
Filled with sediments from Himalayan and Peninsular rivers; alluvial deposits 1,000-2,000 m deep
Physiography of an area: outcome of structure, process and stage of development
Six physiographic divisions: Northern and North-eastern Mountains, Northern Plain, Peninsular Plateau, Indian Desert, Coastal Plains, Islands
Map work: physiographic divisions of India
Himalayas and north-eastern hills; parallel ranges - Great Himalayan range, Trans Himalaya, Middle Himalayas, Shiwalik
Orientation: north-west to south-east in north-west; east-west in Darjeeling and Sikkim; south-west to north-east in Arunachal; north-south in Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram
Approximate length of Great Himalayan range 2,500 km; width 160-400 km
Regional divisions based on relief, alignment and geomorphology

Kashmir or North-western Himalaya: Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar and Pir Panjal ranges; Kashmir valley between Great Himalaya and Pir Panjal; Karewa formations (saffron cultivation); Wular lake; glaciers like Baltoro and Siachen; passes Zoji La, Banihal, Photu La, Khardung La; cold desert of Ladakh; meanders of Jhelum
Peaks and passes for map work: K2 (Godwin Austin), Nanga Parbat

Himachal and Uttarakhand Himalaya: between Ravi and Kali rivers; Great Himalayan range, Lesser Himalaya (Dhaoladhar in HP, Nagtibba in Uttarakhand), Shiwalik; duns (Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun, Patli Dun); hill stations; five prayags; Valley of flowers; Shipki La pass

Darjeeling and Sikkim Himalaya: between Nepal and Bhutan Himalayas; fast flowing rivers (Tista); peaks like Kanchenjunga; Lepcha tribes; duars formations; tea gardens; absence of Shiwalik; Nathu La pass

Arunachal Himalaya: from east of Bhutan Himalaya to Diphu pass; peaks Kangtu and Namcha Barwa; rivers Kameng, Subansiri, Dihang, Dibang, Lohit; tribes (Monpa, Abor, Mishmi, Nyishi, Nagas); jhumming (shifting cultivation)
Eastern hills and mountains: Patkai Bum, Naga hills, Manipur hills, Mizo (Lushai) hills; Barak river; Loktak lake in Manipur
Mountains for map work: Karakoram, Garo-Khasi-Jaintia hills, Aravali, Vindhyan, Satpura, Western and Eastern Ghats
Formed by alluvial deposits of Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; extends about 3,200 km east to west; average width 150-300 km; depth of alluvium 1,000-2,000 m
Three zones north to south: bhabar, tarai and alluvial plains
Bhabar: narrow belt 8-10 km wide at Shiwalik foothills; pebbles and boulders; streams disappear
Tarai: 10-20 km wide south of bhabar; streams re-emerge; marshy, wet; forests; cleared for agriculture
Alluvial plains: old alluvium (bhangar) and new alluvium (khadar); mature stage of fluvial erosion - sand bars, meanders, oxbow lakes, braided channels
Brahmaputra plains known for riverine islands and sand bars; deltaic plains of Ganga-Brahmaputra; delta - sundarbans
Rises 150-600 m above river plains; irregular triangle; Delhi ridge to Rajmahal hills to Gir range to Cardamom hills; Shillong and Karbi Anglong plateau as extension
Features: tors, block mountains, rift valleys, spurs, bare rocky structures, series of hummocky hills, wall-like quartzite dykes; black soil area (Deccan Trap)
Western and north-western part have ravines and gorges (Chambal, Bhind, Morena)
Three broad groups: Deccan Plateau, Central Highlands, North-eastern Plateau
Deccan Plateau: bordered by Western Ghats (Sahyadri) in west, Eastern Ghats in east, Satpura, Maikal range and Mahadeo hills in north
Western Ghats: continuous, higher (900-1,600 m), passes - Thal, Bhor and Pal ghats; peaks Anaimudi (2,695 m, highest peak of Peninsular plateau) and Doddabetta
Eastern Ghats: discontinuous and low, cut by rivers; peaks Mahendragiri; Javadi, Palkonda hills; Nilgiri hills join both Ghats
Central Highlands: bounded by Aravali on west; Satpura range in south formed by series of scarped plateaus; Malwa plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand, Chotanagpur plateau; general elevation 700-1,000 m
Aravali hills: highly eroded relict mountains; Guru Shikhar highest; rivers like Banas, Chambal, Betwa, Ken flowing north-east

North-eastern Plateau: extension of Peninsular block separated by Malda fault; Meghalaya plateau - Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills; Karbi Anglong plateau; Cherrapunji with bare rock surface; mineral rich
Plateaus for map work: Malwa, Chhotanagpur, Meghalaya, Deccan; passes: Shipki La, Nathu La, Palghat, Bhor Ghat, Thal Ghat
North-west of Aravali hills; undulating topography with longitudinal dunes and barchans
Rainfall below 150 mm per year; arid climate with low vegetation (Marusthali)
Evidence that region was under sea during Mesozoic era (wood fossils park at Akal, marine deposits near Brahmsar, Jaisalmer)
Features: mushroom rocks, shifting dunes, oasis; Luni river flowing south-west; inland drainage - streams disappear; brackish lakes (playas) - source of salt
Two divisions: western coastal plains and eastern coastal plains
Western coastal plains: submerged coastal plain (example: city of Dwaraka submerged); narrow belt; natural ports and harbours (Kandla, Mazagaon, JLN port Navha Sheva, Marmagao, Mangalore, Cochin)
Divisions of west coast: Kachchh and Kathiawar coast in Gujarat, Konkan coast in Maharashtra, Goan coast, Malabar coast in Karnataka and Kerala
Malabar coast distinctive feature: kayals (backwaters) used for fishing, inland navigation; Nehru Trophy Vallamkali boat race in Punnamada Kayal, Kerala
Rivers on west coast do not form deltas
Eastern coastal plains: broader, emergent coast with fewer ports and harbours; continental shelf extends up to 500 km into sea
Well-developed deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri on east coast
Coastal plains for map work: Saurashtra, Konkan, North and South Kanara, Malabar, Coromandel, Northern Circar
Two major island groups: Bay of Bengal (about 572 islands) and Arabian Sea
Andaman and Nicobar: between 6 degrees N-14 degrees N and 92 degrees E-94 degrees E; Ritchie's archipelago and Labyrinth island; Ten degree channel separates Andaman (north) from Nicobar (south)
Bay of Bengal islands are elevated portions of submarine mountains; some of volcanic origin - Barren island (only active volcano in India) in Nicobar islands
Mountain peaks: Saddle peak (North Andaman, 738 m), Mount Diavolo, Mount Koyob, Mount Thuiller; coral deposits; equatorial vegetation and convectional rainfall
Arabian Sea islands: Lakshadweep and Minicoy; between 8 degrees N-12 degrees N and 71 degrees E-74 degrees E; about 280-480 km from Kerala coast

Lakshadweep built of coral deposits; about 36 islands, 11 inhabited; Minicoy largest (453 sq km); Eleventh degree channel separates Minicoy from Amini/Cannanore islands; storm beaches with unconsolidated pebbles, shingles
Map work: Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep

Exercise types: MCQs on hills, passes, islands; compare Himalayan and Peninsular regions; bhabar vs tarai; western vs eastern coastal plain; features of Indian desert; draw and label physiographic map
Drainage: flow of water through well-defined channels; drainage system/network
Drainage pattern depends on geological time period, nature and structure of rocks, topography, slope, amount and periodicity of water flow
Catchment area: area drained by a river and its tributaries; drainage basin; watershed - boundary line separating one basin from another
Catchments of large rivers called river basins; small rivulets and rills called watersheds
Difference between river basin and watershed (size and scale)

Important drainage patterns: dendritic (tree branches, e.g. northern plain rivers), radial (from a central hill, e.g. Amarkantak rivers), centripetal (into a lake or depression, e.g. Loktak lake), trellis (primary tributaries parallel and secondary at right angles)
By discharge orientation to sea: Arabian Sea drainage (about 23 percent) and Bay of Bengal drainage (about 77 percent), separated by Delhi ridge, Aravalis and Sahyadris

By size of watershed: major river basins (more than 20,000 sq km catchment, 14 basins - Ganga, Brahmaputra, Krishna, Tapi, Narmada, Mahi, Pennar, Sabarmati, Barak etc.), medium (2,000-20,000 sq km, 44 basins - Kalindi, Periyar, Meghna), minor (less than 2,000 sq km)
By mode of origin, nature and characteristics: Himalayan drainage and Peninsular drainage
Mainly Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra basins; perennial (snow-fed and rain-fed)
Rivers pass through giant gorges carved by erosion simultaneous with uplift; V-shaped valleys, rapids, waterfalls in mountains
In plains: depositional features - flat valleys, oxbow lakes, floodplains, braided channels, deltas at mouth
Highly tortuous courses in plains; frequent shifts in courses (Kosi as 'sorrow of Bihar')
Indo-Brahma or Shiwalik river hypothesis: a mighty river flowed along length of Himalaya from Assam to Punjab into Gulf of Sind in Miocene (5-24 million years ago)
Evidence: lacustrine origin and alluvial deposits of Shiwalik hills (sands, silt, clay, boulders, conglomerates)
Dismemberment into three main drainage systems: Indus and its five tributaries, Ganga, Brahmaputra; due to Pleistocene upheaval in western Himalaya and uplift of Potwar plateau (Delhi ridge)
Downthrusting of Malda gap area between Rajmahal hills and Meghalaya plateau diverted Ganga and Brahmaputra to Bay of Bengal

sections.name: 17.5 River systems of the Himalayan drainage: the Indus

concepts.text: Indus: one of the largest river basins (1,165,000 sq km in total; 321,289 sq km in India); total length 2,880 km (1,114 km in India)
Originates from glacier near Bokhar Chu in Tibetan region at 4,164 m in Kailash range; known as Singi Khamban (Lion's mouth) in Tibet
Flows north-west between Ladakh and Zaskar ranges; passes through Ladakh and Baltistan; enters Pakistan near Chillar in Dardistan
Himalayan tributaries: Shyok, Gilgit, Zaskar, Hunza, Nubra, Shigar, Gasting, Dras; right bank tributaries: Khurram, Tochi, Gomal, Viboa, Sangar (from Sulaiman ranges)
Panjnad tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Satluj - join Indus above Mithankot
Jhelum: rises from spring at Verinag at foot of Pir Panjal; flows through Srinagar and Wular lake; deep narrow gorge
Chenab: largest tributary of Indus; formed by Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi near Keylong in Himachal Pradesh; 1,180 km long
Ravi: rises west of Rohtang pass in Kullu hills; drains Chamba valley
Beas: originates from Beas Kund near Rohtang pass; flows through Kullu valley; joins Satluj near Harike
Satluj: originates in Rakas lake near Mansarovar (Langchen Khambab in Tibet); antecedent river; enters India via Shipki La; feeds Bhakra Nangal project canal
Indus Water Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan: India can use 20 percent of water
Ganga: most important river of India by basin and cultural significance; rises in Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3,900 m) in Uttarkashi as Bhagirathi
Bhagirathi meets Alaknanda at Devaprayag to form Ganga; Alaknanda sources Satopanth glacier above Badrinath; Dhauli and Vishnu Ganga meet at Joshimath (Vishnu Prayag)
Other prayags: Pindar joins at Karna Prayag, Mandakini (Kali Ganga) at Rudra Prayag
Ganga enters plains at Haridwar; flows south, south-east, east; splits into Bhagirathi-Hugli and Padma (Bangladesh)
Length 2,525 km shared by Uttarakhand (110 km), Uttar Pradesh (1,450 km), Bihar (445 km), West Bengal (520 km); basin 8.6 lakh sq km in India - largest in India
Ganga river system with perennial and non-perennial rivers from Himalaya in north and Peninsula in south
Son: major right bank tributary from Amarkantak plateau
Important left bank tributaries: Ramganga, Gomati, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Mahananda

Yamuna: westernmost and longest tributary; source Yamunotri glacier on Bandarpunch range; joins Ganga at Prayag (Allahabad); right bank tributaries Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken from Peninsula; left bank Hindan, Rind, Sengar, Varuna
Chambal: rises near Mhow on Malwa plateau; flows through gorge upwards Kota (Gandhisagar dam); badland topography (Chambal ravines)
Gandak: two streams - Kaligandak and Trishulganga; rises in Nepal Himalaya; joins Ganga at Sonpur near Patna
Ghaghara: originates in Mapchachungo glaciers; tributaries Tila, Seti, Beri; joins Ganga at Chhapra
Kosi: antecedent river; source in north of Mount Everest in Tibet (Arun); main stream; Son Kosi and Tamur Kosi join; 'sorrow of Bihar'
Ramganga: small river rising in Garhwal hills near Gairsain; joins Ganga near Kannauj
Damodar: occupies eastern margins of Chotanagpur plateau through rift valley; Barakar main tributary; once 'sorrow of Bengal'; tamed by Damodar Valley Corporation
Sarda or Saryu: rises in Milam glacier in Nepal Himalaya (Goriganga); called Kali or Chauk; joins Ghaghara
Mahananda: rises in Darjeeling hills; last left bank tributary in West Bengal
Son: large south bank tributary rising in Amarkantak plateau; waterfalls; joins Ganga at Arrah
Brahmaputra: one of the largest rivers in the world; origin in Chemayungdung glacier of Kailash range near Mansarovar lake
Known as Tsangpo (purifier) in Tibet; Rango Tsangpo main right bank tributary in Tibet
Emerges as turbulent river carving deep gorge in central Himalaya near Namcha Barwa (7,755 m); emerges from foothills as Siang or Dihang
Enters India west of Sadiya town in Arunachal Pradesh; left bank tributaries Dibang (Sikang) and Lohit join to form Brahmaputra
Major left bank tributaries: Burhi Dihing, Dhansari (South), Kalang; right bank tributaries: Subansiri (antecedent), Kameng, Manas, Sankosh
Tista joins on right bank in Bangladesh as Jamuna; merges with Padma and falls in Bay of Bengal (Meghna)
Notorious for floods, channel shifting and bank erosion; heavy rain and sediment; riverine islands (Majuli)
Older than Himalayan drainage: broad, largely graded shallow valleys and maturity of rivers
Western Ghats close to west coast act as water divide between major Peninsular rivers draining into Bay of Bengal and small rivulets joining Arabian Sea
Most major Peninsular rivers except Narmada and Tapi flow from west to east
Rivers originating from northern part of Peninsula (Chambal, Sind, Betwa, Ken, Son) belong to Ganga system
Fixed course, absence of meanders, non-perennial flow; Narmada and Tapi flow through rift valleys and form estuaries
Three major geological events: subsidence of western flank of Peninsula leading to submergence below sea (early Tertiary) disturbed symmetrical river plan
Upheaval of Himalayas when northern flank of Peninsular block subsided and resultant trough faulting; Narmada and Tapi flow in trough faults
Slight tilting of Peninsular block from north-west to south-east gave orientation of entire drainage towards Bay of Bengal

sections.name: 17.10 River systems of the Peninsular drainage

concepts.text: Mahanadi: rises near Sihawa in Raipur district of Chhattisgarh; runs through Odisha to Bay of Bengal; length 851 km; basin 1.42 lakh sq km; navigation earlier; 53 percent of basin in MP and Chhattisgarh, 47 percent in Odisha

Godavari: largest Peninsular river (Dakshin Ganga); rises in Nasik district of Maharashtra; length 1,465 km; basin 3.13 lakh sq km (49 percent in Maharashtra); tributaries Penganga, Indravati, Pranhita, Manjra; Polavaram gorge

Krishna: second largest east-flowing Peninsular river; rises near Mahabaleshwar in Sahyadri; length 1,401 km; tributaries Koyna, Tungbhadra, Bhima; basin shared by Maharashtra (27 percent), Karnataka (44 percent), Andhra Pradesh (29 percent)

Kaveri: rises in Brahmagiri hills (1,341 m) of Kogadu district, Karnataka; length 800 km; basin 81,155 sq km; less fluctuation as upper catchment gets rain in SW monsoon and lower in NE monsoon; tributaries Kabini, Bhavani, Amravati; basin shared by Kerala (3 percent), Karnataka (41 percent), Tamil Nadu (56 percent)

Narmada: originates on western flank of Amarkantak plateau (1,057 m); flows in rift valley between Satpura (south) and Vindhyan range (north); Marble rocks gorge and Dhuandhar falls near Jabalpur; length 1,312 km; forms estuary; Sardar Sarovar project
Tapi: west-flowing river rising in Multai, Betul district of Madhya Pradesh; length 724 km; basin 65,145 sq km (79 percent in Maharashtra)
Luni: largest river system of Rajasthan west of Aravali; originates near Pushkar as two branches Saraswati and Sabarmati joining at Govindgarh; ends in Rann of Kachchh; seasonal
