Smaller rivers flowing west: Shetruniji, Bhadra, Dhadhar, Sabarmati, Mahi; Mandovi, Zuari, Sharavati (Jog falls/Gersoppa falls), Bharathapuzha (Ponnani), Periyar (second largest in Kerala), Pamba
Smaller rivers flowing east: Subarnarekha, Baitarni, Brahmani, Vamsadhara, Penner, Palar, Vaigai

Map work: rivers - Brahmaputra, Indus, Satluj, Ganga, Yamuna, Chambal, Damodar, Mahanadi, Krishna, Kaveri, Godavari, Narmada, Tapi, Luni; lakes - Wular, Sambhar, Chilika, Kolleru, Pulicat, Vembanad; Palk Strait, Rann of Kachchh, Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Khambhat

sections.name: 17.11 Comparison of Himalayan and Peninsular rivers

concepts.text: Place of origin: Himalayan mountains covered with glaciers vs Peninsular plateau and central highland
Nature of flow: perennial (glacier and rain) vs seasonal (monsoon rainfall)
Type of drainage: antecedent and consequent leading to dendritic pattern in plains vs super-imposed, rejuvenated resulting in trellis, radial and rectangular patterns
Nature of river: long course flowing through rugged mountains with headward erosion and river capturing vs smaller fixed course with well-adjusted valleys
Catchment area: very large basins vs relatively smaller basins
Age of river: young, youthful, active and deepening valleys vs old rivers with graded profile, almost reached base level
River regime: Himalayan rivers have maximum flow in summer (snow and monsoon) vs Peninsular rivers depend on rainfall

sections.name: 17.12 Extent of usability of river water

concepts.text: Problems in using river water: non-availability of water in sufficient quantity, river water pollution, load of silt, uneven seasonal flow, river water disputes between states, shrinking channels due to extension of settlements
River water pollution by sewage, industrial and agricultural wastes; Ganga and Yamuna highly polluted; Namami Gange programme
Inter-linking of rivers to transfer surplus water to deficit areas; concept and debate

Exercise types: MCQs on river sources and tributaries; river basin vs watershed; drainage patterns identification; evolution of Himalayan and Peninsular drainage; compare Himalayan and Peninsular rivers; map labelling
Weather: momentary state of atmosphere; climate: average of weather conditions over a long period (more than 30 years)
India has a monsoon type of climate, mainly found in South and South-east Asia
Elements of weather and climate: temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, precipitation

sections.name: 18.2 Unity and diversity in the monsoon climate

concepts.text: Monsoon regime emphasises unity of India with rest of South-east Asia
Regional variations in temperature: Rajasthan summer 50 degrees C vs Pahalgam 20 degrees C; Drass winter -45 degrees C vs Thiruvananthapuram 22 degrees C
Variation in precipitation: snowfall in Himalaya, rain elsewhere; Khasi hills over 1,000 cm vs Jaisalmer less than 9 cm
Tamil Nadu coast gets most rain in winter while other parts get rain in June-September
Variation in winds, temperature, rainfall, rhythm of seasons and degree of wetness/dryness creates regional diversity

sections.name: 18.3 Factors determining the climate of India: location and relief

concepts.text: Latitude: Tropic of Cancer divides India; area south tropical, north sub-tropical/temperate
The Himalayan mountains: barrier protecting from cold northern winds; trap monsoon winds and force them to shed moisture
Distribution of land and water: Indian Ocean in south and continuous mountains in north; differential heating causes different air pressure, reversal of monsoon winds
Distance from the sea: coastal areas have equable climate; interior experiences extremes (continentality)
Altitude: temperature decreases with height; Agra vs Darjeeling example
Relief: physiography affects temperature, air pressure, direction and speed of wind and rainfall distribution; windward vs leeward sides of Western Ghats and Assam hills

sections.name: 18.4 Factors related to air pressure and winds

concepts.text: Three factors: distribution of air pressure and winds on surface; upper air circulation (jet streams); western cyclonic disturbances and tropical cyclones
Mechanism of weather in winter season: surface pressure and winds - high pressure north of Himalaya; dry continental winds blow from north-west
Jet stream: westerly jet stream above 9-13 km over Asia in winter; divided into two branches by Tibetan highlands; southern branch over India
Western cyclonic disturbances: originate over Mediterranean Sea, brought by westerly jet stream; cause winter rain in north-west India
Tropical cyclones originate in Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean in October-December; high winds, heavy rain; hit Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha coasts
Mechanism of weather in summer: shift of ITCZ to 20-25 degrees N over Gangetic plain (monsoon trough); westerly jet withdraws; easterly jet stream over peninsula
Easterly jet stream steers tropical depressions into India; their tracks are areas of highest rainfall
Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ): low pressure zone at equator where trade winds converge; moves north in summer
Monsoon: seasonal reversal in wind direction; understanding through ship observations, satellite data and research (MONEX)
Onset of the monsoon: differential heating of land and sea (Halley's classical theory); shift of ITCZ; role of Tibetan plateau heating; easterly jet; southern oscillation
Monsoon is pulled-in by thermal low over north-west India and Pakistan; SE trades cross equator, deflected to become SW monsoon
Onset over Kerala around 1 June; reaches Mumbai and Kolkata around 10-13 June; covers whole country by mid-July

El Nino and the Indian monsoon: El Nino is a warm ocean current along Peru coast in some years; causes distortion of equatorial atmospheric circulation, irregular evaporation and reduced plankton; used for long-range forecasting
Southern Oscillation (SO): pressure seesaw between Indian Ocean and Pacific; ENSO; reversal of pressure conditions linked to weak monsoon
Entering of the monsoon: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches
Rain-bearing systems and rainfall distribution: tropical depressions from Bay of Bengal; west coast rain orographic (offshore vortices, troughs)

Break in the monsoon: spells of rain alternating with dry spells; caused by changes in monsoon trough position (axis near foothills), fewer tropical depressions; west coast dry when winds blow parallel to coast

sections.name: 18.6 The rhythm of seasons: cold weather season

concepts.text: Four seasons by meteorologists: cold weather, hot weather, south-west monsoon, retreating monsoon
Cold weather season: from mid-November to February; December and January coldest; mean temperature below 21 degrees C in north; cold waves and frost; 'cold desert' Ladakh
Temperature: decreases from south to north; Peninsula has no well-defined cold season due to moderating sea influence (24-25 degrees C)

Pressure and winds: by end of December high pressure over north-west; winds blow from land to sea - north-east trade winds; Tamil Nadu receives rain from these winds after picking moisture over Bay of Bengal
Rainfall: winter rain from western disturbances in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, western UP (useful for rabi crops); snowfall in Himalayas; 'mahawat' in north-west
Rainfall decreases from west to east in plains and increases from west to east in Himalayan region

sections.name: 18.7 The rhythm of seasons: hot weather season

concepts.text: From March to May; temperature rises northward with sun's apparent movement; 45 degrees C in north-west in May
Temperature in peninsular India moderated by ocean; highest temperature in Deccan 38 degrees C; hill stations cooler due to altitude
Pressure and winds: ITCZ shifts north; low pressure over north-west and central India; loo - hot dry winds in north and north-western India

Local storms of hot weather season: Mango shower (Kerala and coastal Karnataka, ripening mangoes), Blossom shower (coffee flowers in Kerala), Nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi in Bengal - useful for tea, jute, rice; 'bardoli chheerha' in Assam), Loo (hot dry winds in northern plains)

sections.name: 18.8 The rhythm of seasons: southwest monsoon season

concepts.text: Low pressure intensifies over north-western India by early June attracting trade winds from southern hemisphere; SW monsoon arrives
Burst of monsoon: sudden onset of rain with violent thunder and lightning
Monsoon winds cover country in about a month
Two branches: Arabian Sea branch and Bay of Bengal branch

Monsoon winds of Arabian Sea: three branches - one obstructed by Western Ghats giving heavy rain on windward side (250-400 cm), rain-shadow on leeward (Deccan); second strikes Narmada and Tapi valleys to central India and Chotanagpur; third strikes Saurashtra peninsula and Kachchh, then Rajasthan along Aravali - very little rain, joins Bay of Bengal branch in Punjab and Haryana

Monsoon winds of Bay of Bengal: strike Myanmar coast and south-east Bangladesh; deflected towards India by Arakan Hills; enter West Bengal and Bangladesh; one branch moves along Ganga plains westward, another moves up Brahmaputra valley giving heavy rain in north-east (Khasi hills - Mawsynram highest rainfall)
Tamil Nadu coast remains dry during this season: parallel to Bay of Bengal branch and in rain-shadow of Arabian Sea branch

Characteristics of monsoonal rainfall: derived from SW monsoon June-September; governed by relief; declining rainfall with distance from sea (Kolkata 119 cm to Bikaner 24 cm); heavy rainfall spells interrupted by breaks; uneven distribution, often torrential causing floods and soil erosion; variability causes droughts and floods; uncertain onset and withdrawal

sections.name: 18.9 The rhythm of seasons: season of retreating monsoon

concepts.text: October and November: monsoon trough weakens and gets replaced by high pressure; monsoon withdraws gradually
Withdrawal from north-west India by early October; from rest of country by early December
Clear skies and rise in temperature; land still moist; 'October heat' due to hot humid conditions
Low pressure shifts to Bay of Bengal by early November; cyclonic depressions from Andaman Sea cross east coast causing heavy rain in Krishna, Godavari, Kaveri deltas; frequently destructive
Bulk of rainfall of Coromandel coast derived from these depressions and cyclones
Traditional six two-month seasons: Vasanta (spring), Grishma (summer), Varsha (rainy), Sharad (autumn), Hemanta (pre-winter), Shishira (winter)
Table: Indian traditional seasons with corresponding Indian and English months
Average annual rainfall about 125 cm with great spatial variation
Areas of high rainfall (over 200 cm): west coast, Western Ghats, sub-Himalayan areas of north-east, hills of Meghalaya; parts of Khasi and Jaintia hills over 1,000 cm

Areas of medium rainfall (100-200 cm): southern parts of Gujarat, east Tamil Nadu, north-eastern Peninsula (Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, eastern MP), northern Ganga plain along sub-Himalaya and Cachar valley, Manipur
Areas of low rainfall (50-100 cm): western UP, Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, eastern Rajasthan, Gujarat and Deccan plateau
Areas of inadequate rainfall (less than 50 cm): parts of Peninsula (Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra), Ladakh and most of western Rajasthan
Snowfall restricted to Himalayan region
Variability of rainfall: coefficient of variation formula C.V. = (standard deviation / mean) x 100
Variability over 50 percent in western Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir, interior Deccan; less than 25 percent on west coast, Western Ghats, north-east, Ganga plains
Map reading: annual rainfall map and rainfall variability map; areas of highest and lowest rainfall and temperature for map work

sections.name: 18.12 Monsoon and the economic life in India

concepts.text: Monsoon as axis around which entire agricultural cycle revolves; about 64 percent depend on agriculture for livelihood
Except Himalayas, all parts have temperature above threshold for crops/plants year round
Variability of monsoon climate introduces variety of crops
Variability of rainfall brings droughts or floods every year
Agricultural prosperity depends on timely and adequately distributed rain; failure hits areas without irrigation
Sudden monsoon burst creates soil erosion problem over large areas
Winter rainfall by temperate cyclones in north India highly beneficial for rabi crops
Regional climatic variation reflected in food, clothes and house types
Climate is changing due to natural and human-induced causes; greenhouse gases rising (carbon dioxide), causing global warming
Rise in temperature affects polar ice caps and mountain glaciers; rise in sea level would submerge coastal areas and islands (Maldives, low-lying deltas)
Mean annual surface temperature rose about 0.6 degrees C in twentieth century; projected rise by 2100
Concern: carbon dioxide concentration rising since industrial revolution; need to reduce emissions

Exercise types: MCQs on seasons and local storms; factors determining climate; mechanism of monsoon and role of jet streams and El Nino; why Tamil Nadu gets winter rain; rainfall distribution and variability; monsoon and economic life
Natural vegetation: plant community left undisturbed for long, allowing species to adjust to climate and soil
Distinction between forest (wild) and planted vegetation (gardens, orchards)
Variation in India: Himalayan temperate vegetation, Western Ghats and Andaman tropical rain forests, delta mangroves, Rajasthan desert cacti and thorny bushes
Factors: climate (rainfall, temperature) and soil
Five major forest types: tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen; tropical deciduous; tropical thorn; montane; littoral and swamp
Map work: vegetation types of India on outline map
Found in western slope of Western Ghats, hills of north-eastern region and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Conditions: annual precipitation over 200 cm, mean annual temperature above 22 degrees C
Well stratified structure; trees reach 60 m or above; no definite time for leaf fall - evergreen appearance
Species: rosewood, mahogany, aini, ebony
Semi-evergreen forests in less rainy parts; species white cedar, hollock and kail
Colonial impact: commercial exploitation; railway sleepers from chir pine replacing oak in Garhwal and Kumaon; clearing for tea, rubber and coffee plantations
Most widespread forests of India; monsoon forests; rainfall 70-200 cm
Moist deciduous (100-200 cm rainfall): north-eastern states along Himalayan foothills, eastern slopes of Western Ghats and Odisha; teak, sal, shisham, hurra, mahua, amla, semul, kusum, sandalwood
Dry deciduous (70-100 cm rainfall): rainier parts of Peninsula and plains of UP and Bihar; tendu, palas, amaltas, bel, khair, axlewood
Trees shed leaves in dry season; forest appears like vast grassland with naked trees
Western and southern Rajasthan: sparse cover due to low rainfall and overgrazing
Occur where rainfall is less than 50 cm
Areas: semi-arid south-west Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
Plants leafless for most of year, scrub appearance; tussocky grass up to 2 m as undergrowth
Species: babool, ber, wild date palm, khair, neem, khejri, palas
Decrease in temperature with altitude causes change in vegetation; northern mountain forests and southern mountain forests
Himalayan zonation: deciduous forests in foothills; wet temperate forests (oak, chestnut) at 1,000-2,000 m
Chir pine at 1,500-1,750 m; deodar - highly valued endemic species mainly in western Himalaya, durable wood for construction
Chinar and walnut sustain Kashmir handicrafts; blue pine and spruce at 2,225-3,048 m
Silver firs, junipers, pines, birch and rhododendrons at 3,000-4,000 m; alpine forests and pastures; mosses and lichens as tundra at higher reaches
Temperate grasslands; transhumance by Gujjars, Bakarwals, Bhotiyas and Gaddis
Southern slopes of Himalayas carry thicker vegetation than northern slopes (more precipitation)

Southern mountain forests: Western Ghats, Vindhyas and Nilgiris; temperate forests called sholas in Nilgiris, Anaimalai and Palani hills; magnolia, laurel, cinchona and wattle; also in Satpura and Maikal ranges
India has rich wetland habitats (3.9 million hectares); about 70 percent of wetlands under paddy cultivation
Ramsar Convention (international convention on wetlands); Chilika lake (Odisha) and Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur) as protected habitats of waterfowl

Eight categories of wetlands in India (reservoirs of Deccan and lagoons of south-west coast; saline expanses of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Gulf of Kachchh; freshwater lakes of Gujarat-Rajasthan-MP; delta wetlands of east coast; freshwater marshes of Gangetic plain; floodplains of Brahmaputra and north-east; Kashmir and Ladakh lakes; mangroves of Andaman and Nicobar)
Mangroves: grow along coasts in salt marshes, tidal creeks, mud flats and estuaries; halophytic (salt-tolerant) plants; shelter birds
Mangroves cover 6,740 sq km in India - 7 percent of world's mangroves; Andaman and Nicobar, Sundarbans (West Bengal), deltas of Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna
Encroachment on mangroves and need for conservation

sections.name: 19.8 Forest cover in India and forest conservation

concepts.text: Forest area (land notified as forest, legal) vs forest cover (actual area under forest canopy, from satellite imagery)
Forests' direct and indirect economic and social benefits
National Forest Policy 1952, modified in 1988; emphasis on sustainable forest management
Policy aims: bring 33 percent geographical area under forest; maintain environmental stability and restore ecology; conserve natural heritage and genetic pool
Policy aims: check soil erosion, extension of desert lands, reduce floods and droughts; increase forest cover through social forestry and afforestation on degraded land
Policy aims: increase productivity of forests for timber, fuel, fodder and food for rural population; encourage substitution of wood; people's movement involving women to plant trees and stop felling
